analysis.one_liner: Forces big beef packers to publish their cattle contracts and buy a minimum share of cattle through open bidding.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action; it sat in the House Agriculture Committee and its livestock subcommittee from March 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the largest beef packing companies to file every type of contract they use to buy cattle — including premiums and discounts — into a public library USDA would maintain, with a monthly report on how many cattle are committed under them. It would also divide the country into regions and require those big packers to buy a minimum share of cattle through open, negotiated bidding rather than behind-closed-doors formula contracts, with fines of up to $90,000 per week for violations. The point is to give cattle ranchers better price information and bargaining power in a market dominated by a handful of buyers.
analysis.who_benefits: Cattle ranchers and feedlot operators who sell to packers. They would see the actual contract terms packers use, and a guaranteed share of sales would happen through open competitive bidding instead of formula prices tied to thin negotiated markets. Consumers benefit indirectly if better price discovery and competition discipline beef prices.

how_it_helps.text: USDA must build and maintain a public library of every type of contract between packers and producers for buying fed cattle, including schedules of premiums and discounts, and publish a monthly report on commitments.

USDA must create five to seven regions covering the continental United States and set a mandatory minimum percentage of cattle that covered packers must buy through approved pricing mechanisms — negotiated purchases, negotiated grid purchases, stockyards, or open trading platforms — from producers who are not packers.

A covered packer is defined as any packer that slaughtered 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle on average over the prior five years, so the rules target the largest buyers while smaller regional plants are exempt.
Packers violating the mandatory minimum face civil penalties of up to $90,000 per violation, with each continuing week counted as a separate violation.

The bill also tightens reporting: packers must report cattle scheduled for delivery over the next 14 days by 10 a.m. the following day, USDA must publish expedited daily carcass weights, and cutout yield data at least annually.

analysis.who_pays: The largest beef packing companies, which would bear compliance costs for contract disclosure and reporting, would have to shift a share of purchases into negotiated channels, and would face fines for falling short. Some of that cost could be passed along in beef prices.

drawbacks.text: Forcing a set percentage of purchases into negotiated channels limits the flexibility of the formula and contract arrangements that both packers and some producers rely on for predictable volume and delivery, and USDA would have two years of rulemaking discretion to set the regional minimums, with room to get them wrong.

Compliance and reporting requirements imposed on packers add costs that could be passed through to consumers in higher beef prices, and the bill authorizes unspecified appropriations to USDA to run the contract library and reporting systems.

The bill's own text acknowledges packers that use negotiated market prices as the basis for formula contracts have incentives to limit participation in price discovery — meaning the effectiveness of the mandate depends on vigorous enforcement rather than the disclosure alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is modest and targeted: publish the contracts, and require the biggest buyers to transact a minimum share in the open. The costs — compliance, rulemaking, some loss of contracting flexibility — are real but limited, and the potential upside for ranchers' bargaining power in a highly concentrated buying market is substantial. The bill leans on USDA discretion and enforcement to work, which is its main design risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Agriculture Committee, which sent it to its livestock subcommittee, and neither held a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Feenstra introduced the Cattle Price Discovery and Transparency Act of 2023 on March 1, 2023, with cosponsors named in the bill text.
The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture the same day it was introduced.
On April 4, 2023, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry.
No further action was taken — no subcommittee vote, no full committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest beef packing companies are better off: the contract disclosure requirements and negotiated-purchase minimums that would have applied to them never took effect, and the concentrated buying market they operate in was left unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Randy Feenstra
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed for cattle price transparency and mandatory negotiated-purchase minimums.

for.name: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as named in the introduced text.

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry and never scheduled a markup or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Largest beef packing companies
against.role: Covered packers slaughtering 5%+ of the nation's fed cattle
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory price-discovery requirements and contract library legislation targeting the largest packers throughout the cattle-industry policy debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Republican and one Democratic cosponsor in the House, but it died in committee under Republican control without ever reaching a vote, so no roll call ever showed where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Large beef packers (the firms slaughtering 5% or more of U.S. fed cattle)
industries.note: The bill would force them to disclose every contract type they use, route a minimum share of purchases through open bidding, and pay fines up to $90,000 per week for shortfalls. Their interest in keeping the current system runs against ranchers who want transparent, competitive pricing.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and feedlot operators
industries.note: They would gain access to the actual contract terms and premium/discount schedules packers use, plus a guaranteed share of open-market bidding, strengthening their bargaining position on price.
As packers below the 5% national slaughter threshold, they are exempt from the mandatory minimums, giving them flexibility their giant competitors would not have.
Better price discovery and competition among buyers could help restrain beef prices, but compliance costs passed through by packers could work the other way.
